reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / DeVita's Cancer: Principles & Practice of Oncology
clinicalPearls: Most oral cavity cancers are squamous cell carcinomas driven by tobacco in all its forms, betel or areca nut chewing, and heavy alcohol use, which act synergistically
It typically presents as a persistent ulcer, red or white patch, lump, or non-healing sore in the mouth, often with pain, bleeding, or loose teeth as disease advances
Any oral lesion that fails to heal within a few weeks should be biopsied rather than treated repeatedly as trauma or infection
Premalignant lesions such as leukoplakia, erythroplakia, and oral submucous fibrosis carry malignant potential and warrant monitoring and biopsy
Cervical lymph node metastasis is common and significantly worsens prognosis, so neck examination and imaging are integral to staging
Surgical resection with adequate margins is the mainstay for most tumours, often combined with neck dissection and reconstruction depending on extent
Radiotherapy, with or without chemotherapy, is used adjuvantly for adverse features or as definitive treatment in selected cases
Treatment can markedly affect speech, swallowing, and appearance, so multidisciplinary rehabilitation and dental assessment before radiotherapy are important
reference.pathophysiology: Oral squamous cell carcinoma arises from the mucosal lining of the oral cavity through cumulative genetic damage caused by carcinogens in tobacco, areca nut, and alcohol. This produces field cancerisation with premalignant changes such as leukoplakia and erythroplakia that can progress through dysplasia to invasive carcinoma. The tumour invades local structures including muscle, bone, and nerves, and spreads readily to regional cervical lymph nodes; distant metastasis occurs later. Chronic mucosal irritation and conditions such as oral submucous fibrosis further predispose to malignant change.
additionalDifferentials: Traumatic ulcer from dentures or a sharp tooth
Aphthous ulceration or other benign oral ulcers
Oral leukoplakia or erythroplakia without invasion
Infective causes such as fungal or specific granulomatous lesions
Salivary gland or other non-squamous oral tumours
additionalInvestigations: Thorough inspection and palpation of the oral cavity and neck with biopsy of the lesion
CT or MRI to assess local extent, bony invasion, and nodal disease
Chest imaging and PET-CT for distant staging and second primaries
Examination under anaesthesia and panendoscopy where indicated to map extent and exclude synchronous tumours
Dental assessment and nutritional evaluation before treatment
redFlags: A mouth ulcer or lesion that fails to heal within a few weeks
A firm, fixed, or enlarging cervical lymph node
Unexplained loosening of teeth, numbness, or difficulty moving the tongue
Persistent oral bleeding, pain, or difficulty swallowing with weight loss
reference.prognosis: Prognosis depends on stage, tumour thickness, and nodal status; early localised tumours have good cure rates, whereas nodal metastasis, deep invasion, and advanced stage substantially reduce survival and increase recurrence.
pitfalls: Repeatedly treating a persistent oral ulcer as trauma or infection without biopsy
Neglecting to examine and image the cervical lymph nodes
Overlooking premalignant lesions that require surveillance
Failing to arrange dental and rehabilitation input before and after treatment
references: DeVita's Cancer: Principles & Practice of Oncology
management: Confirm diagnosis with clinic biopsy of the primary lesion, plus flexible laryngoscopy to assess the airway and exclude a second primary tumour.

Stage with contrast-enhanced CT of the maxillofacial region, neck, and chest, or PET-CT with a diagnostic neck CT; reserve MRI for dental artefact, suspected perineural invasion, or marrow involvement from bone invasion.

Discuss every case at a head and neck multidisciplinary tumour board (surgery, radiation oncology, medical oncology, radiology, pathology, plus dentistry, speech-language pathology, dietetics, physical therapy) before finalising a treatment plan.

Biopsy any oral ulcer, red or white patch, or non-healing sore that fails to resolve with conservative care, rather than repeatedly treating it as trauma or infection; keep leukoplakia, erythroplakia, and (per general head and neck standard of care, not DeVita-specific) oral submucous fibrosis under surveillance with biopsy if they change.

Favour primary surgical resection for most resectable oral cavity disease; use radiotherapy mainly in the adjuvant setting and add chemotherapy to radiotherapy only in selected cases based on pathological findings, not as a routine third arm.

For early superficial lesions, prefer surgical resection over primary radiotherapy given the comparative risk of soft tissue or bone necrosis, dental damage, and xerostomia with radiotherapy; for some early lip lesions, surgery and radiotherapy can be equally curative and the choice is guided by cosmetic and functional factors.

For moderately advanced and advanced disease, combine resection (with mandibulectomy or more extensive surgery as needed), neck dissection, reconstruction, and postoperative radiotherapy or chemoradiotherapy guided by pathology; T4 disease can still be cured with aggressive multimodal treatment, though functional outcomes are more variable.

Manage lip cancer with simple excision for small lower lip lesions away from the commissure, and consider radiotherapy for commissure involvement, larger lesions, or upper lip carcinomas; treat advanced lip lesions with resection, neck dissection, reconstruction, and adjuvant radiotherapy, adding chemotherapy for more advanced disease.
Use frozen-section margin control intraoperatively and pursue further resection for positive margins when feasible.

Base the neck management plan on depth of invasion and clinical nodal status: consider elective ipsilateral (and, for deeper or higher-risk tumours, contralateral) neck dissection for a clinically negative neck, and address levels I through IV (adding level V for multilevel disease) for a clinically node-positive neck; extend to bilateral treatment for floor-of-mouth, soft palate or base of tongue extension, midline proximity, or deep invasion.

Aim for an adequate neck dissection yield and consider adjuvant radiotherapy or closer observation when yield is low; factor node number, size, laterality, and extranodal extension into the decision for postoperative neck irradiation.

Consider definitive chemoradiotherapy or radiotherapy alone for locally advanced disease when extensive surgery cannot be tolerated or function-preserving surgery is not feasible, while keeping surgery-first as the default for resectable disease.

For recurrent, unresectable, or metastatic disease, apply general head and neck squamous cell carcinoma systemic therapy principles (chemotherapy, EGFR-targeted therapy, or immunotherapy), noting this follows general oncology standards rather than DeVita's oral cavity chapter.

During follow-up, biopsy any post-radiotherapy ulcer that fails a trial of conservative management or has a rolled or elevated border, and repeat or deepen biopsy if suspicion persists despite a negative result; manage new nodal disease in a previously untreated neck with dissection followed by postoperative radiotherapy or chemoradiotherapy, and arrange dental and nutritional assessment before treatment, particularly before radiotherapy.
